To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

EHR use is associated with improved glycated hemoglobin and low density liproprotein cholesterol levels in patients with diabetes, and that this association is larger for patients with diabetes who are cared for by higher cohesive primary care teams.
EHR use is associated with improvements in clinical outcomes for diabetes patients and that these improvements are larger in magnitude for patients with higher levels of primary care team cohesion.
EHR use in primary care was associated with improvements in clinical outcomes for diabetes patients.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the organizational context affects the relationship between EHRs and patient care outcomes.
the impact of the EHR on diabetes care quality, and the role that team cohesion plays in this relationship.
the impact of the electronic health records (HER) and teamwork on diabetes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
EHRs can have a positive impact on clinical outcomes, but this impact may be dependent upon the team cohesion of the care delivery team.
electronic health record use was associated with improvements in diabetes care quality, but that these improvements were greater in practices where primary care teams had higher levels of cohesion.

EHR use was not associated with statistically significant improvements in A1C or LDL C levels for patients with diabetes, but EHR use was significantly associated with improvements in A1 C and LDL C levels for diabetes patients with higher cohesion teams.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the use of EHRs in the context of high cohesion primary care teams is associated with greater health outcome improvement for patients with diabetes than EHR use in the context of low cohesion primary care teams.
team cohesion may be a key component of the organizational context in the use of EHRs.
EHRs can have a positive impact on clinical outcomes, but this impact is moderated by the degree to which the primary care teams use the EHRs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
EHRs are a tool, and their effectiveness depends on the context of their use.
EHR use may be more beneficial in primary care teams with higher cohesion.
EHR implementation may have a larger impact on clinical outcomes when providers practice within a high cohesion primary care team.
